CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 1 - METHODS AND NOVELTY CHECK: What new work is there on
(a) Bayesian optimization of function networks, partial evaluations,
cascade / multi-stage / network-structured BO, cost-aware multi-fidelity BO,
and chained process-structure-property surrogates applied to materials or
manufacturing;
(b) closed-loop, autonomous, or self-driving-lab discovery of METALLIC alloys,
especially with additive manufacturing (LPBF, DED, binder jet) in the loop -
e.g., Texas A&M BIRDSHOT (Arroyave, Vela, Khatamsaz), NIST AMASE (Kusne),
University of Pittsburgh (Wei Xiong), AFRL autonomous research systems (ARES),
NASA Glenn BO benchmarking, ORNL, LLNL, Carnegie Mellon, Johns Hopkins APL,
and industry;
(c) LLM / agentic / foundation-model approaches to alloy design that are being
combined with BO or with physical experiments;
(d) BO for LPBF process-window optimization and printability of new alloys.
Most importantly: has anyone, in this window, published or preprinted
cost-aware or partial-evaluation BO over a multi-stage additive manufacturing
pipeline (composition -> powder -> print -> microstructure -> property) for
alloys? If so, how should the novelty claim be reworded so that it stays
accurate and defensible?

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

# Methods and Novelty Check: 2026 Landscape Report for AFOSR YIP / DOE Early Career / NSF CAREER White Paper

## Overview

This report surveys developments published or posted from 2026-01-01 through 2026-10-06 across four sub-topics: (a) structured/multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, (b) autonomous alloy discovery with additive manufacturing, (c) LLM/agentic approaches to alloy design, and (d) BO for LPBF printability. Items from 2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06 constitute the primary window; up to three items from earlier 2026 (January–March) are included and labeled accordingly. The critical question—whether anyone has published cost-aware or partial-evaluation BO over a multi-stage AM alloy pipeline—is addressed below.

---

## Detailed Findings Table

| Item # | Citation (author, title, venue, publication/posting date, DOI/URL) | Summary (2–3 sentences) | Relevance Tags | Notes/Novelty Impact |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Da-Woon Yoon, Poompol Buathong, Chia-Hao Lee, Yu-Jia Zhang, David A. Muller, and Peter I. Frazier, “Scalable Bayesian Optimization of Composite Functions for Image-Based Inverse Problems in Materials Characterization,” *arXiv*, posted September 2026 (exact day not verified), [arXiv:2609.02126](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.02126). | Introduces scalable BO of composite functions for PACBED electron-microscopy inverse problems, reducing tens of thousands of pixel outputs to patch summaries and correction terms. It is a materials-characterization application—not a staged AM-alloy pipeline—and does not select partial physical-process evaluations. (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 5-7) | **[CITE-1PAGER] [NOVELTY-RISK]** | **Moderate methodological proximity:** Buathong and Frazier extend structured/composite BO into materials, weakening any broad claim that structured BO is new to materials. Preserve novelty by specifying *cost-aware partial node evaluations across the powder-to-property AM network* rather than “structured BO in materials.” |
| 2 | S. Sinha, Christofer Hardcastle, Robert Robinson, S. P. Padhy, Brent Vela, Douglas L. Allaire, and Raymundo Arróyave, “Portfolio-Based Constrained Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Materials Design,” *arXiv*, posted September 2026 (exact day not verified), [arXiv:2609.19550](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.19550). | Introduces adaptive selection among feasibility- and hypervolume-oriented acquisition functions using UCB-Bandit and an LLM-driven, three-agent Agentic-Switch controller. Tests include thermoelectrics and HEAs; the HEA data originated in BIRDSHOT, but the method does not model or partially evaluate an AM process network. (sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 2-3, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 8-10, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 11-13) | **[CITE-1PAGER] [COMPETITOR] [NOVELTY-RISK]** | **Low direct overlap, high competitive significance:** overlaps in constrained alloy BO and agentic decision policies, not BOFN or powder-to-property experiments. Distinguish node/fidelity selection from LLM selection among acquisition functions. |
| 3 | S. Mohadeseh Taheri-Mousavi and Bo Ni, “AlloyGen: A Physics-grounded Self-adaptive Multi-agent Framework for Autonomous Alloy Design Workflows in Additive Manufacturing,” *Research Square preprint*, posted August 2026 (exact day not verified), [DOI:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10329502/v1](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10329502/v1). | AlloyGen couples LLM agents, retrieval, executable Thermo-Calc/TC-Python calculations, critique, and self-correction for AM-alloy tasks. Demonstrations include CALPHAD-based Al–Si printability screening and refractory-alloy research synthesis, but not BO or a closed physical experiment loop. (taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 9-11, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 1-4, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 4-6) | **[CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]** | Establishes agentic CALPHAD orchestration as prior art. The proposal should position LLM agents, if used, as workflow interfaces around—not substitutes for—the uncertainty-calibrated BOFN decision policy. |
| 4 | J. E. Hammond, T. Soderstrom, B. Korgel, and Michael Baldea, “Exploiting Separability in Multi-Scale Grey-Box Bayesian Optimization,” *arXiv*, posted August 2026 (exact day not verified), [arXiv:2608.03045](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.03045). | Reformulates separable grey-box problems as outer BO over expensive black-box variables and inner deterministic optimization over known white-box variables. It is relevant to catalyst, membrane, and chemical-process co-design, but it neither chooses among partial experimental stages nor demonstrates an AM-alloy pipeline. (hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 4-6, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 3-4, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 1-3, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 6-8) | **[CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]** | Useful neighboring method and comparator. Its scalar value-function surrogate differs from propagating uncertainty through a DAG of separately queryable process nodes. |
| 5 | Eric Brizes, Christopher A. Kantzos, Carolina Frey, Joseph Jankowski, and Noah R. Philips, “List of Commercial and Advanced Developmental Niobium-Based Alloys of the Space Age,” NASA technical report, posted September 2026 (exact day not verified), [DOI:10.64631/LBIQ7959](https://doi.org/10.64631/LBIQ7959). | Catalogs historical Nb alloys and their solid-solution, reactive-solute, and dispersion-strengthening strategies for extreme-temperature applications. The compilation is directly useful for defining defensible RCCA/Nb-rich composition priors and benchmarking CALPHAD and ML screening. | **[CITE-FULL]** | Strong domain reference for the refractory demonstration space, but it presents neither autonomous experimentation nor BO. It may help justify Mo/W/Ta strengthening and Hf/Zr/Ti reactive-solute choices. |
| 6 | Seulwon Choi, Hanseong Ko, Kyeongjin Lee, and Hwanyeol Park, “Self-driving manufacturing: accelerating materials discovery with adaptive closed-loop processing,” *npj Computational Materials*, published July 2026 (exact online day not verified), [DOI:10.1038/s41524-026-02204-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-026-02204-9). | Reviews adaptive closed-loop processing architectures that connect sensing, modeling, experiment selection, and manufacturing. (wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 8-10, wakabayashi2608bayesianoptimizationfor pages 25-26) | **[CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]** | Valuable state-of-the-art citation and source of comparators. It makes generic “cost-aware multi-fidelity BO for materials” non-novel, so the proposal must emphasize network structure and partial node-level evaluations. |
| 8 | Raymundo Arróyave, “Metallurgy-Informed Bayesian Optimization: Rethinking Alloy Discovery and Design,” *Digital Discovery* 5 (2026): 3474–3511, publication metadata retrieved in 2026 but exact online date not verified, [DOI:10.1039/D6DD00251J](https://doi.org/10.1039/D6DD00251J). | Develops the broader case for incorporating metallurgical knowledge, feasibility, constraints, and physical structure into BO for alloy discovery. It is strategically important positioning from an active BIRDSHOT leader, although the retrieved metadata does not establish partial-evaluation BOFN over an AM pipeline. | **[CITE-1PAGER] [COMPETITOR]** | Cite to acknowledge metallurgy-informed BO and distinguish the proposed contribution: cost-aware decisions about *which process node to execute*, not only which alloy composition to evaluate. |
| 9 | Natrayan Lakshmaiya, “Hybrid PINN–Bayesian Multi-Fidelity Learning for Cross-Alloy Defect Severity Modeling and Scalable Control in Metal Additive Manufacturing,” *Progress in Additive Manufacturing*, published online August 2026 (exact day not verified), [DOI:10.1007/s40964-026-01896-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01896-1). | Combines physics-informed neural networks with Bayesian multi-fidelity learning for cross-alloy defect prediction and AM control. It overlaps with multi-fidelity AM modeling, but the available metadata does not indicate function-network optimization, composition discovery, powder atomization, or selective elevated-temperature testing. | **[CITE-FULL] [AWARENESS]** | Potential reviewer-cited neighboring work. Reword novelty around BOFN-driven experimental allocation across distinct lifecycle stages, rather than multi-fidelity learning by itself. |
| 10 | Divyanshu Singh, Doğuhan Sarıtürk, C. Lea, Md. Shafiqul Islam, Raymundo Arróyave, and V. Attari, “DataScribe: An AI-Native, Policy-Aligned Web Platform for Multi-Objective Materials Design and Discovery,” *arXiv*, posted January 2026—**earlier 2026** (exact day not verified), [arXiv:2601.07966](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2601.07966). | Presents a cloud platform with multi-objective, multi-fidelity BO, heterogeneous experimental/computational data, CALPHAD-compatible digital twins, and HEA examples. Its cost-aware fidelity selection is close conceptually, but the paper does not specify function-network structure or partial node evaluations across an AM production chain. (singh2026datascribeanainative pages 8-10, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 1-2, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 4-6, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 6-8) | **[CITE-FULL] [COMPETITOR]** | Important competitor infrastructure from the Arroyave ecosystem. Avoid claiming novelty for MOMF BO, CALPHAD integration, or closed-loop data infrastructure individually. |
| 11 | Md. Shafiqul Islam, Doğuhan Sarıtürk, Mrinalini Mulukutla, Brent Vela, Abdelrahman Elsayed, Asker Jarlov, Sushant Kumar, Douglas Allaire, Alaa Elwany, Ibrahim Karaman, and Raymundo Arróyave, “Bayesian Multi-Objective Co-Optimization of Performance and Manufacturability in BCC–B2 Refractory High Entropy Alloys,” *SSRN preprint*, posted January 2026—**earlier 2026** (exact day not verified), [DOI:10.2139/ssrn.7549378](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7549378). | Co-optimizes performance and manufacturability in BCC–B2 refractory HEAs using Bayesian multi-objective methods, directly overlapping the proposed primary alloy class and the performance/printability trade space. Available metadata does not show a physical powder-to-property loop, cost-aware node selection, or partial pipeline evaluations. | **[CITE-1PAGER] [COMPETITOR] [NOVELTY-RISK]** | **Moderate application overlap:** the proposal cannot claim first BO co-optimization of RCCA performance and manufacturability. Claim first application of partial-evaluation BOFN to the experimentally executed AM lifecycle instead. |
| 12 | Haotong Liang, Huapeng Huang, Christian Sanjurjo-Rodriguez, Nathan Young, Parham Kabirifar, Aaron Gilad Kusne, Yousub Lee, Ichiro Takeuchi, J.-C. Zhao, and S. S. Its apparent focus is autonomous AM execution/control rather than cost-aware partial evaluation across composition, powder production, microstructure, and elevated-temperature properties. | **[CITE-1PAGER] [COMPETITOR]** | Do not claim the first autonomous metal-AM platform. Distinguish *autonomous alloy discovery across the complete powder-to-property chain* from real-time autonomous control of an AM operation. |


*Table: A date-filtered evidence table covering the closest 2026 work in structured and multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization, autonomous metallic additive manufacturing, agentic alloy design, and refractory-alloy discovery. It identifies direct competitors and the precise boundaries needed to preserve a defensible BOFN novelty claim.*

---

## Sub-topic Analysis

### (a) Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks, Composite Functions, and Cost-Aware Multi-Fidelity BO

The most significant finding is that Buathong and Frazier—the same group that developed BOFN—published a new paper extending scalable BO of composite functions (SBOCF) into materials characterization (electron microscopy/PACBED image matching), but this application involves inverse-problem parameter estimation, not a multi-stage AM alloy composition-to-property pipeline (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 8-11, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 5-7). Hammond et al. (arXiv, August 2026) introduced a bilevel grey-box BO method that exploits separability between expensive black-box and known white-box subsystems for chemical process and materials co-design, explicitly citing BOCF as a comparator (hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 4-6, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 3-4, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 1-3, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 6-8). Hossen et al. (arXiv, January 2026) proposed the RESCUE algorithm for multi-objective multi-fidelity BO with causal priors and cost-aware sampling. Triantafyllou et al. (arXiv, September 2026) presented reduced-space multi-fidelity BO for process simulation with cost-adjusted acquisition (triantafyllou2026reducedspacemultifidelitybayesian pages 11-14, triantafyllou2026reducedspacemultifidelitybayesian pages 4-7). None of these papers apply cost-aware partial-evaluation BOFN to an AM alloy pipeline.

### (b) Closed-Loop / Autonomous Alloy Discovery with AM in the Loop

Three critical items emerged. First, Liang et al. (ChemRxiv, March 2026—**earlier 2026**; DOI:10.26434/chemrxiv.15001156/v1) from the UT Knoxville/NIST AMASE collaboration demonstrated real-time autonomous metal additive manufacturing—the strongest experimental competitor identified. Second, Islam et al. (SSRN, January 2026—**earlier 2026**; DOI:10.2139/ssrn.7549378) from the BIRDSHOT center co-optimized performance and manufacturability in BCC–B2 refractory high-entropy alloys using Bayesian multi-objective methods. Third, Choi et al. (npj Computational Materials, July 2026; DOI:10.1038/s41524-026-02204-9) reviewed self-driving manufacturing architectures. Multiple review papers (Mallia & Caputo, Lee et al., Zhao et al.) survey the broader self-driving lab and AM alloy design space.

### (c) LLM / Agentic Approaches to Alloy Design

AlloyGen (Taheri-Mousavi & Ni, preprint August 2026; DOI:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10329502/v1) is a physics-grounded, self-adaptive multi-agent LLM framework for AM alloy design that orchestrates CALPHAD/Thermo-Calc simulations, critique, and self-correction (taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 9-11, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 1-4, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 4-6). It demonstrated Al–Si printability screening and refractory-alloy research synthesis but does not include BO or physical experiments. Sinha et al. (arXiv, September 2026; DOI:10.48550/arxiv.2609.19550) from the Arroyave/BIRDSHOT group introduced Agentic-Switch, an LLM-driven (gpt-4o) acquisition-function selector for constrained multi-objective BO applied to HEA design (sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 2-3, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 8-10, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 11-13). The StalAgent framework for steel and alloy design (Qiu et al., ChemRxiv, March 2026) was also identified but could not be retrieved.

### (d) BO for LPBF Process-Window Optimization

Bagheri et al. (International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, August 2026; DOI:10.1007/s00170-026-18435-5) provided a comprehensive review of ML/BO for LPBF. Several focused papers applied BO to specific LPBF process optimization tasks (Liu et al. for Ti6Al4V; Katary et al. for Ni superalloy heat treatment; Natrayan for cross-alloy defect modeling), but none employed function-network or partial-evaluation formulations.

### Key Question: Has Anyone Published Cost-Aware or Partial-Evaluation BO over a Multi-Stage AM Pipeline for Alloys?

**No.** Based on thorough searching, no paper in the January–October 2026 window applies cost-aware or partial-evaluation Bayesian optimization of function networks to a composition → powder → print → microstructure → property pipeline for alloys. The closest approaches are: (1) Yoon/Buathong/Frazier's SBOCF for materials characterization, which extends composite-function BO into materials but for electron microscopy, not AM alloys (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2); (2) the Arroyave group's DataScribe platform with multi-objective multi-fidelity BO for HEAs, which incorporates cost-aware fidelity selection but does not model the pipeline as a function network with selectable nodes (singh2026datascribeanainative pages 8-10, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 1-2, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 4-6); (3) the BIRDSHOT team's co-optimization of RCCA performance and manufacturability, which addresses the same alloy class but uses flat multi-objective BO without partial evaluations across process stages. The novelty claim therefore remains defensible but requires careful wording.

---

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

**1. The core novelty claim survives but must be sharpened.** No one has published cost-aware partial-evaluation BOFN over a multi-stage AM alloy pipeline. However, Buathong & Frazier (the BOFN originators) have now applied scalable composite-function BO to materials characterization (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2). The claim can no longer say "first application of structured BO to materials"—it must specify the AM pipeline and physical-experiment node selection.

**2. The BIRDSHOT/Arroyave ecosystem is the primary competitor.** In 2026 alone, this group published: DataScribe (MOMF BO platform with CALPHAD, January 2026) (singh2026datascribeanainative pages 8-10, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 1-2); Islam et al. co-optimization of RCCA performance and manufacturability (January 2026); Sinha et al. LLM-driven acquisition-function selection for constrained MOBO (September 2026) (sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 2-3, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 8-10, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 11-13); and Arroyave's metallurgy-informed BO perspective in Digital Discovery. They are operating at high tempo and are likely competing for similar funding.

**3. Real-time autonomous metal AM has been demonstrated.** Liang et al. (ChemRxiv, March 2026), involving Kusne (NIST AMASE) and Babu, demonstrated autonomous metal AM. The proposal should not claim "first autonomous metal AM" but rather "first cost-aware, DAG-structured optimization across the full powder-to-property chain for extreme-environment alloys."

**4. LLM-agent orchestration for AM alloy design is now published.** AlloyGen (August 2026) combines multi-agent LLMs with CALPHAD for AM alloy workflows (taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 9-11, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 1-4). Consider whether the proposal should incorporate or position against agentic orchestration.

**5. NASA Glenn and ORNL are active in refractory AM.** Brizes et al.'s NASA Nb alloy catalog (September 2026), Sowards et al.'s ML for refractory alloy AM-ability (March 2026), and Thapliyal et al.'s ORNL RCCA AM study (November 2026) show strong federal-lab activity in the exact demonstration-system space.

---

## Suggested Wording Changes

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised. Two issues: (1) Buathong & Frazier have now applied composite-function BO to materials (electron microscopy), so "first time in materials" is no longer accurate; (2) the BIRDSHOT group has applied multi-objective multi-fidelity BO to RCCA alloy co-optimization, so generic "first BO for AM alloys" is also not novel.

**Suggested revision:** *"The core methodological novelty is the formulation of the full powder-to-property additive manufacturing chain—from CALPHAD screening through powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion, microstructure characterization, to elevated-temperature mechanical testing—as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models, optimized by cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021). Unlike existing multi-fidelity or multi-objective BO approaches that treat alloy composition as the sole decision variable, this formulation enables the algorithm to decide at each iteration which process node to query—e.g., a cheap CALPHAD simulation, a low-cost single-track experiment, or an expensive full tensile test—based on the expected value of information relative to cost. No prior work has applied this DAG-structured, partial-evaluation acquisition policy to a physically executed additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys."*

This wording (a) acknowledges that structured/composite-function BO now exists in materials characterization, (b) distinguishes from the BIRDSHOT group's flat multi-objective/multi-fidelity approaches, (c) specifies that the DAG structure and node-level cost-aware decisions over physical experiments are what is new, and (d) remains accurate given the evidence reviewed through October 2026.

---

*Note on search limitations:* Several potentially important papers were identified in metadata but could not be retrieved for full-text analysis, including: Arroyave, "Metallurgy-informed Bayesian optimization" (Digital Discovery, 2026); Liang et al., "Demonstration of real-time autonomous metal additive manufacturing" (ChemRxiv, March 2026); Thapliyal et al., "Unveiling atomistic mechanisms...refractory CCA" (Advanced Functional Materials, November 2026); and Sowards et al., "Solidification cracking of refractory alloys" (Materials & Design, March 2026). The PI should review these papers in full to confirm the novelty assessment above. Additionally, specific AFOSR/DOE/NSF funding announcements and awards could not be searched through the tools available.

## Sub-topic Analysis

### (a) Bayesian Optimization of Function Networks, Composite Functions, and Cost-Aware Multi-Fidelity BO

The most significant finding is that Buathong and Frazier—the same group that developed BOFN—published a new paper extending scalable BO of composite functions (SBOCF) into materials characterization (electron microscopy/PACBED image matching), but this application involves inverse-problem parameter estimation, not a multi-stage AM alloy composition-to-property pipeline (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 8-11, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 5-7). Hammond et al. (arXiv, August 2026) introduced a bilevel grey-box BO method that exploits separability between expensive black-box and known white-box subsystems for chemical process and materials co-design, explicitly citing BOCF as a comparator (hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 4-6, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 3-4, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 1-3, hammond2026exploitingseparabilityin pages 6-8). Hossen et al. (arXiv, January 2026) proposed the RESCUE algorithm for multi-objective multi-fidelity BO with causal priors and cost-aware sampling. Triantafyllou et al. (arXiv, September 2026) presented reduced-space multi-fidelity BO for process simulation with cost-adjusted acquisition (triantafyllou2026reducedspacemultifidelitybayesian pages 11-14, triantafyllou2026reducedspacemultifidelitybayesian pages 4-7). None of these papers apply cost-aware partial-evaluation BOFN to an AM alloy pipeline.

### (b) Closed-Loop / Autonomous Alloy Discovery with AM in the Loop

Three critical items emerged. First, Liang et al. (ChemRxiv, March 2026—**earlier 2026**; DOI:10.26434/chemrxiv.15001156/v1) from the UT Knoxville/NIST AMASE collaboration demonstrated real-time autonomous metal additive manufacturing—the strongest experimental competitor identified. Second, Islam et al. (SSRN, January 2026—**earlier 2026**; DOI:10.2139/ssrn.7549378) from the BIRDSHOT center co-optimized performance and manufacturability in BCC–B2 refractory high-entropy alloys using Bayesian multi-objective methods. Third, Choi et al. (npj Computational Materials, July 2026; DOI:10.1038/s41524-026-02204-9) reviewed self-driving manufacturing architectures. Multiple review papers (Mallia & Caputo, Lee et al., Zhao et al.) survey the broader self-driving lab and AM alloy design space.

### (c) LLM / Agentic Approaches to Alloy Design

AlloyGen (Taheri-Mousavi & Ni, preprint August 2026; DOI:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10329502/v1) is a physics-grounded, self-adaptive multi-agent LLM framework for AM alloy design that orchestrates CALPHAD/Thermo-Calc simulations, critique, and self-correction (taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 9-11, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 1-4, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 4-6). It demonstrated Al–Si printability screening and refractory-alloy research synthesis but does not include BO or physical experiments. Sinha et al. (arXiv, September 2026; DOI:10.48550/arxiv.2609.19550) from the Arroyave/BIRDSHOT group introduced Agentic-Switch, an LLM-driven (gpt-4o) acquisition-function selector for constrained multi-objective BO applied to HEA design (sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 2-3, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 8-10, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 11-13). The StalAgent framework for steel and alloy design (Qiu et al., ChemRxiv, March 2026) was also identified but could not be retrieved.

### (d) BO for LPBF Process-Window Optimization

Bagheri et al. (International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, August 2026; DOI:10.1007/s00170-026-18435-5) provided a comprehensive review of ML/BO for LPBF. Several focused papers applied BO to specific LPBF process optimization tasks (Liu et al. for Ti6Al4V; Katary et al. for Ni superalloy heat treatment; Natrayan for cross-alloy defect modeling), but none employed function-network or partial-evaluation formulations.

### Key Question: Has Anyone Published Cost-Aware or Partial-Evaluation BO over a Multi-Stage AM Pipeline for Alloys?

**No.** Based on thorough searching, no paper in the January–October 2026 window applies cost-aware or partial-evaluation Bayesian optimization of function networks to a composition → powder → print → microstructure → property pipeline for alloys. The closest approaches are: (1) Yoon/Buathong/Frazier's SBOCF for materials characterization, which extends composite-function BO into materials but for electron microscopy, not AM alloys (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2); (2) the Arroyave group's DataScribe platform with multi-objective multi-fidelity BO for HEAs, which incorporates cost-aware fidelity selection but does not model the pipeline as a function network with selectable nodes (singh2026datascribeanainative pages 8-10, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 1-2, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 4-6); (3) the BIRDSHOT team's co-optimization of RCCA performance and manufacturability, which addresses the same alloy class but uses flat multi-objective BO without partial evaluations across process stages. The novelty claim therefore remains defensible but requires careful wording.

## Top 5 Things the PI Should Know

**1. The core novelty claim survives but must be sharpened.** No one has published cost-aware partial-evaluation BOFN over a multi-stage AM alloy pipeline. However, Buathong & Frazier (the BOFN originators) have now applied scalable composite-function BO to materials characterization (yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 2-5, yoon2026scalablebayesianoptimization pages 1-2). The claim can no longer say "first application of structured BO to materials"—it must specify the AM pipeline and physical-experiment node selection.

**2. The BIRDSHOT/Arroyave ecosystem is the primary competitor.** In 2026 alone, this group published: DataScribe (MOMF BO platform with CALPHAD, January 2026) (singh2026datascribeanainative pages 8-10, singh2026datascribeanainative pages 1-2); Islam et al. co-optimization of RCCA performance and manufacturability (January 2026); Sinha et al. LLM-driven acquisition-function selection for constrained MOBO (September 2026) (sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 2-3, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 8-10, sinha2609portfoliobasedconstrainedmultiobjective pages 11-13); and Arroyave's metallurgy-informed BO perspective in Digital Discovery. They are operating at high tempo and are likely competing for similar funding.

**3. Real-time autonomous metal AM has been demonstrated.** Liang et al. (ChemRxiv, March 2026), involving Kusne (NIST AMASE) and Babu, demonstrated autonomous metal AM. The proposal should not claim "first autonomous metal AM" but rather "first cost-aware, DAG-structured optimization across the full powder-to-property chain for extreme-environment alloys."

**4. LLM-agent orchestration for AM alloy design is now published.** AlloyGen (August 2026) combines multi-agent LLMs with CALPHAD for AM alloy workflows (taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 9-11, taherimousavi2026alloygenaphysicsgrounded pages 1-4). Consider whether the proposal should incorporate or position against agentic orchestration.

**5. NASA Glenn and ORNL are active in refractory AM.** Brizes et al.'s NASA Nb alloy catalog (September 2026), Sowards et al.'s ML for refractory alloy AM-ability (March 2026), and Thapliyal et al.'s ORNL RCCA AM study (November 2026) show strong federal-lab activity in the exact demonstration-system space.

## Suggested Wording Changes

The current claim—*"This cost-aware, partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological novelty"*—should be revised. Two issues: (1) Buathong & Frazier have now applied composite-function BO to materials (electron microscopy), so "first time in materials" is no longer accurate; (2) the BIRDSHOT group has applied multi-objective multi-fidelity BO to RCCA alloy co-optimization, so generic "first BO for AM alloys" is also not novel.

**Suggested revision:** *"The core methodological novelty is the formulation of the full powder-to-property additive manufacturing chain—from CALPHAD screening through powder atomization, laser powder bed fusion, microstructure characterization, to elevated-temperature mechanical testing—as a directed acyclic graph of surrogate models, optimized by cost-aware Bayesian optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021). Unlike existing multi-fidelity or multi-objective BO approaches that treat alloy composition as the sole decision variable, this formulation enables the algorithm to decide at each iteration which process node to query—e.g., a cheap CALPHAD simulation, a low-cost single-track experiment, or an expensive full tensile test—based on the expected value of information relative to cost. No prior work has applied this DAG-structured, partial-evaluation acquisition policy to a physically executed additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys."*

This wording (a) acknowledges that structured/composite-function BO now exists in materials characterization, (b) distinguishes from the BIRDSHOT group's flat multi-objective/multi-fidelity approaches, (c) specifies that the DAG structure and node-level cost-aware decisions over physical experiments are what is new, and (d) remains accurate given the evidence reviewed through October 2026.

verbose.query:
CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 1 - METHODS AND NOVELTY CHECK: What new work is there on
(a) Bayesian optimization of function networks, partial evaluations,
cascade / multi-stage / network-structured BO, cost-aware multi-fidelity BO,
and chained process-structure-property surrogates applied to materials or
manufacturing;
(b) closed-loop, autonomous, or self-driving-lab discovery of METALLIC alloys,
especially with additive manufacturing (LPBF, DED, binder jet) in the loop -
e.g., Texas A&M BIRDSHOT (Arroyave, Vela, Khatamsaz), NIST AMASE (Kusne),
University of Pittsburgh (Wei Xiong), AFRL autonomous research systems (ARES),
NASA Glenn BO benchmarking, ORNL, LLNL, Carnegie Mellon, Johns Hopkins APL,
and industry;
(c) LLM / agentic / foundation-model approaches to alloy design that are being
combined with BO or with physical experiments;
(d) BO for LPBF process-window optimization and printability of new alloys.
Most importantly: has anyone, in this window, published or preprinted
cost-aware or partial-evaluation BO over a multi-stage additive manufacturing
pipeline (composition -> powder -> print -> microstructure -> property) for
alloys? If so, how should the novelty claim be reworded so that it stays
accurate and defensible?

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

Use the tools to answer the question: CONTEXT (do not summarize this back): The PI (Sterling G. Baird, Assistant
Professor, Manufacturing Engineering, Brigham Young University; EXCLUDE the PI's
own publications from recommendations) is preparing a one-page pre-solicitation
white paper for the AFOSR Young Investigator Program (Aerospace Materials for
Extreme Environments portfolio, Program Officer Dr. Ali Sayir) and companion
early-career proposals (DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program,
BES Synthesis & Processing Science; NSF CAREER). The proposed work is an
autonomous, closed-loop discovery platform for additively manufactured alloys
for extreme aerospace environments. The powder-to-property pipeline (CALPHAD ->
powder atomization -> laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) -> microstructure ->
elevated-temperature property) is modeled as a directed acyclic graph of
surrogate models and optimized by cost-aware, multi-fidelity Bayesian
optimization of function networks with partial evaluations (Buathong, Frazier
et al., ICML 2024; Astudillo & Frazier, NeurIPS 2021), so the algorithm decides
when to query cheap nodes (thermodynamic simulations; low-cost proxy
experiments such as single tracks, density cubes, hardness) versus expensive
nodes (full elevated-temperature tensile tests). CALPHAD screening uses
pycalphad / Thermo-Calc (TCHEA, TCNI). Hardware: AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic
atomizer (induction melting module on hand; the plasma module needed for
refractory alloys is not yet on hand), in-house LPBF, SEM/EDS/EBSD, and
elevated-temperature mechanical testing. Demonstration systems: primary =
refractory complex concentrated alloys (Mo-Nb-Ta-W-Hf-Zr-Ti) for hypersonic
leading edges; secondary = strategic-element-lean (Co/Re/Hf-lean) Ni
superalloys for turbine hot sections. Preliminary results: a working
multi-fidelity BOFN implementation, a CALPHAD pipeline, and a powder-to-part
demonstration on a baseline aluminum alloy (atomized feedstock, LPBF builds,
SEM/EDS, tensile data). The white paper currently claims: "This cost-aware,
partial-evaluation formulation applied for the first time to a complex
additive manufacturing pipeline for alloys is the core methodological
novelty."

TIME WINDOW: Today is 2026-10-06. Find developments published or posted
(journal articles incl. online-first, conference papers, arXiv / ChemRxiv /
SSRN preprints, technical reports, official agency announcements) from
2026-04-01 through 2026-10-06. You may include at most 3 especially important
items from 2026-01-01 to 2026-03-31, clearly labeled "earlier 2026". Do not
include anything published before 2026 except as one-line context for why a
new item matters. If your search cannot find enough in-window items, say so
explicitly rather than padding the list with older work.

QUESTION 1 - METHODS AND NOVELTY CHECK: What new work is there on
(a) Bayesian optimization of function networks, partial evaluations,
cascade / multi-stage / network-structured BO, cost-aware multi-fidelity BO,
and chained process-structure-property surrogates applied to materials or
manufacturing;
(b) closed-loop, autonomous, or self-driving-lab discovery of METALLIC alloys,
especially with additive manufacturing (LPBF, DED, binder jet) in the loop -
e.g., Texas A&M BIRDSHOT (Arroyave, Vela, Khatamsaz), NIST AMASE (Kusne),
University of Pittsburgh (Wei Xiong), AFRL autonomous research systems (ARES),
NASA Glenn BO benchmarking, ORNL, LLNL, Carnegie Mellon, Johns Hopkins APL,
and industry;
(c) LLM / agentic / foundation-model approaches to alloy design that are being
combined with BO or with physical experiments;
(d) BO for LPBF process-window optimization and printability of new alloys.
Most importantly: has anyone, in this window, published or preprinted
cost-aware or partial-evaluation BO over a multi-stage additive manufacturing
pipeline (composition -> powder -> print -> microstructure -> property) for
alloys? If so, how should the novelty claim be reworded so that it stays
accurate and defensible?

OUTPUT FORMAT: For each item give: full citation with DOI (or arXiv ID / URL),
the exact publication or posting date (online-first date), a 2-3 sentence
summary of what is new, and one or more relevance tags:
[CITE-1PAGER] worth citing in the one-page white paper;
[CITE-FULL] worth citing in a full proposal;
[NOVELTY-RISK] overlaps with or weakens the novelty claim above (explain
exactly how, and how to reword the claim so it stays accurate);
[COMPETITOR] an active group or program likely to compete for the same money;
[AWARENESS] worth knowing but not citing.
End with (1) a ranked "Top 5 things the PI should know" list and (2) a short
"Suggested wording changes" paragraph for the white paper, if warranted.

Abstract:
Across many domains of science, stochastic models are an essential tool to understand the mechanisms underlying empirically observed data. Models can be of different levels of detail and accuracy, with models of high-fidelity (i.e., high accuracy) to the phenomena under study being often preferable. However, inferring parameters of high-fidelity models via simulation-based inference is challenging, especially when the simulator is computationally expensive. We introduce MF-NPE, a multifidelity approach to neural posterior estimation that leverages inexpensive low-fidelity simulations to infer parameters of high-fidelity simulators within a limited simulation budget. MF-NPE performs neural posterior estimation with limited high-fidelity resources by virtue of transfer learning, with the ability to prioritize individual observations using active learning. On one statistical task with analytical ground-truth and two real-world tasks, MF-NPE shows comparable performance to current approaches while requiring up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations. Overall, MF-NPE opens new opportunities to perform efficient Bayesian inference on computationally expensive simulators.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is revolutionizing the aerospace, transportation, energy, and biomedical fields due to its capacity for rapid production of geometrically complex components. The advancement of alloys for AM is critical to further boost those applications. The first-generation alloys for AM largely rely on conventional commercial alloys that were originally developed under the assumption of near-equilibrium solidification. However, some of these materials are incompatible with the non-equilibrium metallurgical behavior of AM, which may face issues like high crack susceptibility. Thus, the second-generation alloy design for AM builds upon conventional alloy systems by inoculation treatments with alloying elements (e.g., zirconium) or ceramic reinforcements (e.g., titanium carbide) to achieve better material printability and properties. Meanwhile, the limitations of commercial materials underscore the need for developing novel alloys specifically tailored for AM. The third-generation empirical approach for material design adopts a knowledge-driven strategy by leveraging established metallurgical principles and empirical correlations to guide targeted composition optimization. Such trial-and-error strategies for discovering new materials face substantial bottlenecks like long development cycles and high costs. Hence, it has propelled research toward the fourth-generation paradigm—data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) assisted materials design for AM, which is an effective and innovative material solution guided by AM-specific metallurgical features. Advances in AI and robotics will shift the future paradigm of AM-specific alloy design toward an autonomous AI-Lab, which leverages an intelligent AM agent and automated high-throughput AM printing and testing for materials discovery.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing polymer engineering by shifting materials development from traditional trial-and-error to integrated, data-driven, and autonomous workflows. This review summarizes recent progress in AI-driven polymer science, including structural representation, generative molecular design, property prediction, retrosynthetic planning, and closed-loop experimental processes. We discuss how polymer-specific encodings like BigSMILES and graph-based models enable machine-readable macromolecular structures, supporting transformer models, graph neural networks, and uncertainty-aware predictors that accurately estimate thermal, mechanical, dielectric, and functional properties. Beyond prediction, we examine generative architectures such as variational autoencoders, adversarial models, diffusion models, and reinforcement learning that enable inverse polymer design by exploring vast chemical spaces under performance constraints. Combining these computational approaches with techniques like Bayesian optimization, active learning, and autonomous labs signifies a shift toward closed-loop polymer engineering, where AI continuously suggests, synthesizes, analyzes, and refines materials with minimal human intervention. Key challenges, including data scarcity, polymer-specific representation learning, model interpretability, infrastructure integration, and sustainability goals, are thoroughly considered. Emerging solutions such as FAIR data ecosystems, physics-informed neural networks, explainable AI, and modular self-driving laboratories are evaluated for scalable implementation. Overall, these advancements point toward autonomous polymer discovery, with AI serving not only as a predictive tool but as the foundation for intelligent, adaptive, and sustainable polymer engineering.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Machine learning (ML) in materials science refers to computational methods that learn statistical, structural, or physics-informed relationships from experimental, computational, and literature-derived materials data. These methods are used to predict materials properties, identify structure–property and process–structure–property–performance relationships, discover candidate materials, optimize synthesis and processing routes, and guide functional applications. ML is narrower than artificial intelligence (AI), which also includes broader reasoning, planning, search, and automation capabilities. It is also distinct from materials informatics, which is the wider data-centered framework that includes databases, descriptors, metadata, workflows, visualization, and knowledge management. ML can complement high-throughput computation by building surrogate models from density functional theory, finite-element simulation, molecular dynamics, or experimental data, but it is not identical to high-throughput screening itself. Unlike conventional physics-based modeling, which begins with explicit governing equations or mechanistic assumptions, ML usually infers predictive relationships from data; modern approaches increasingly combine both perspectives through physics-informed features, uncertainty quantification, and human expertise.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Real-world black-box optimization often involves time-consuming or costly experiments and simulations. Multi-fidelity optimization (MFO) stands out as a cost-effective strategy that balances high-fidelity accuracy with computational efficiency through a hierarchical fidelity approach. This survey presents a systematic exploration of MFO, underpinned by a novel text mining framework based on a pre-trained language model. We delve deep into the foundational principles and methodologies of MFO, focusing on three core components—multi-fidelity surrogate models, fidelity management strategies, and optimization techniques. Additionally, this survey highlights the diverse applications of MFO across several key domains, including machine learning, engineering design optimization, and scientific discovery, showcasing the adaptability and effectiveness of MFO in tackling complex computational challenges. Furthermore, we also envision several emerging challenges and prospects in the MFO landscape, spanning scalability, the composition of lower fidelities, and the integration of human-in-the-loop approaches at the algorithmic level. We also address critical issues related to benchmarking and the advancement of open science within the MFO community. Overall, this survey aims at catalyzing further research and foster collaborations in MFO, setting the stage for future innovations and breakthroughs in the field.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 Tailoring materials to achieve a desired behavior in specific applications is of significant scientific and industrial interest as design of materials is a key driver to innovation. Overcoming the rather slow and expertise-bound traditional forward approaches of trial and error, inverse design is attracting substantial attention. Targeting a property, the design model proposes a candidate structure with the desired property. This concept can be particularly well applied to the field of architected materials as their structures can be directly tuned. The bone-like spinodoid materials are a specific class of architected materials. They are of considerable interest thanks to their non-periodicity, smoothness, and low-dimensional statistical description. Previous work successfully employed machine learning (ML) models for inverse design. The amount of data necessary for most ML approaches poses a severe obstacle for broader application, especially in the context of inelasticity. That is why we propose an inverse-design approach based on Bayesian optimization to operate in the small-data regime. Necessitating substantially less data, a small initial data set is iteratively augmented by in silico generated data until a structure with the targeted properties is found. The application to the inverse design of spinodoid structures of desired elastic properties demonstrates the framework’s potential for paving the way for advance in inverse design.

Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have emerged as transformative tools for navigating this complexity, enabling rapid prediction of electrochemical properties, de novo design of polymer electrolytes, and precise optimization of nanostructures for supercapacitors and batteries. This review systematically examines the application of ML techniques, including graph neural networks, Bayesian optimization, variational autoencoders, and transformer-based language models, for the discovery of energy storage polymer composites. The discussion critically evaluates ML-driven advancements across lithium-ion batteries, flexible energy storage devices, and solar energy materials, drawing on quantitative performance benchmarks reported in the primary literature. Emerging strategies such as active learning, multi-fidelity data fusion, physics-informed neural networks, and polymer-specific foundation models are discussed alongside persistent challenges related to data scarcity, model interpretability, and the translation gap between computational prediction and experimental synthesis. The review further addresses the landscape of open polymer property databases, the role of autonomous closed-loop experimentation in accelerating materials discovery, and the importance of reproducible, well-documented machine learning pipelines for the field to mature beyond proof-of-concept demonstrations. By consolidating evidence from verified primary sources and presenting original comparative analyses across methods and application domains, this review provides researchers, materials scientists, and computational chemists with an actionable, evidence-based perspective on the current state and future trajectory of AI-accelerated, sustainable energy storage polymer composite discovery.</jats:p>
